The Survey cites strong outcomes: ~25,000 nudged under the Foreign Asset Campaign with 61% positive response, leading to ₹29,000+ crore in foreign assets and ₹1,000+ crore in foreign income declared; 91,000+ updated returns for Section 80GGC cutting inflated deductions by ~₹2,050 crore and generating ₹680+ crore extra tax; fixes to HRA claims adding ₹119+ crore; and TDS nudges where 8,500+ entities revised returns, adding 1.08 crore deductees and ~₹4,825 crore additional TDS. Overall, it frames nudging as a low-friction, preventive model that reduces disputes and compliance costs while improving trust and revenue.

HMRC has published guidance for software developers on what responsible use of generative AI should look like in commercial tax products that help people submit returns or information to HMRC. It says AI-enabled tax software should be transparent about where AI is used and its limits, reliable by drawing on high-quality and up-to-date sources such as HMRC guidance, legislation and case law, and kept under human control by prompting users to review outputs and reminding them they remain responsible for accuracy. HMRC also expects strong security and privacy protections because of sensitive data, and ethical design that is fair, trustworthy, accountable, and clearly serving the public good.
The African nation takes a major step to simplifying investment procedures with the launch of its new eRegulations investment portal – with support from UN Trade and Development and partners

UNCTAD will launch a new “IIA Facilitation Mapping Database” on 12 August to help countries track and implement international investment facilitation commitments. The tool maps 400+ international investment agreements (since 2010), including the WTO Investment Facilitation for Development Agreement finalized in November 2023, giving governments a consolidated view of overlapping obligations and where treaty provisions align (e.g., transparency) or diverge (e.g., procedural simplification). Built on UNCTAD’s IIA Navigator and developed with input from leading universities, it is intended to improve transparency, guide policy ahead of forums like the World Investment Forum 2026 and the WTO’s 14th Ministerial Conference, and help UNCTAD tailor technical assistance—supported by funding from the Netherlands.

The Laredo Police Department (LPD) is expanding AI and tech tools in 2026 to improve reporting, response times and records access while coping with staffing shortages. Planned rollouts include CaseX (AI-assisted online reporting, beta in March), Peregrine (mid-March data/records integration across divisions), and Prepare911 (April automated non-emergency triage that can route emergencies to 911 and share live caller coordinates and audio to nearby officers for faster self-deployment). LPD is also using gunfire-location cameras, crash-detection sensors, Skydio drones, and Flock “shot/crash spotter” systems—emphasizing human review and responsible use of AI.

The UK government announced it has recruited a Meta-funded team of AI specialists to develop open-source AI tools aimed at improving public services, including transport maintenance, public safety, and defence/national security decision-making. Over the next year, the team—made up of experts from places like the Alan Turing Institute and universities—will build systems that public authorities can run without depending on closed commercial platforms, helping keep sensitive data in-house. Meta said the work may use open-source models such as its Llama system, while the resulting tools will be owned by the UK government so departments can customize them as needed.

A DHS inventory of AI use cases for 2025 says ICE is using Palantir’s generative AI to speed up how it reviews public immigration-enforcement tips submitted through its tip form. The tool sorts, categorizes, translates non-English submissions, and produces a short “BLUF” (bottom-line-up-front) summary using commercially available large language models without extra training on agency data, aiming to reduce manual review work and help investigators act faster on urgent leads. The inventory lists the system as operational since May 2, 2025, and reporting suggests it may be connected to updates to ICE’s longstanding Palantir-backed tipline and case management tools.

The UK is launching Police.AI, a new national AI centre for policing backed by £115m Home Office funding, designed to speed up and standardise the development, testing, and rollout of AI tools across all 43 police forces in England and Wales.

The Tampa Police Department says it is rolling out several AI-enabled technologies in 2026 to improve public safety and officer effectiveness. These include “Prepared 911” for faster call handling, real-time multilingual translation, and secure live video streaming from callers’ phones; expanded body-worn camera tools like Axon Assistant and Policy Chat for on-the-spot translation and voice-activated policy guidance with official citations; VR immersive training pods that use AI-driven characters and realistic simulations to practice communication and de-escalation; and a Drone as First Responder program that can launch immediately after a 911 call to provide early aerial intelligence before officers arrive. The department says these tools aim to boost response speed, reduce language barriers, strengthen training, and support safer, better-informed decisions in the field.

Singapore’s Monetary Authority (MAS) is working with banks on what could be the world’s first nationwide rollout of FIDO hardware security tokens for online banking, especially to approve high-value transactions. The move responds to rising phishing losses (reported to have grown from about S$7.3m in H1 2023 to about S$30m in H1 2025) and aims to boost trust by using cryptographic keys stored on a physical device (making phishing much harder without the token). However, it may add friction for users, create support burdens (setup, lost devices, replacement), and won’t stop scams that rely on fake merchant sites unless wider ecosystems also adopt stronger authentication.

The UK government says an AI- and analytics-led push delivered its “biggest ever fraud crackdown,” saving a record £480m in the year to April 2025, and is now positioning the Fraud Risk Assessment Accelerator (FRAA) as the next step: a generative AI tool that scans draft policies to spot exploitable weaknesses before programs launch, with early tests suggesting up to 80% faster fraud-risk identification. But investigations leader Tony McClements argues AI alone won’t meaningfully change outcomes without enough trained investigators and, crucially, prosecutions to create deterrence; he also criticizes the post-pandemic NATIS response as ineffective. Overall, the debate highlights a shift toward preventive, AI-driven fraud control, while raising concerns that prevention must be matched with enforcement and accountability to stop repeat offenders.

Researchers at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy (the Evidence for Justice Lab) launched the Justice AI Tracker (JAI-T) — an interactive website that collects publicly available information to show where and how AI is being piloted, tested, or implemented across law enforcement, courts, and corrections in the 100 largest U.S. cities. It’s intended to fill a transparency gap until more governments publish formal AI inventories, and to support accountability and public understanding. The lab highlighted common AI use cases it is tracking, including facial recognition, gun detection, automatic license plate readers, body-camera footage review, and non-emergency dispatch assistance. Future updates (expected in about six months) aim to add vendor details and community insights, with additional reporting planned.

India’s Ministry of Law and Justice has launched Nyaya Setu on WhatsApp (from 1 Jan 2026) to give citizens free, quick legal guidance through a chatbot-style service. It offers basic help and pointers across common areas like family and matrimonial matters, property/tenancy issues, and other general legal queries, aiming to make “ease of justice” accessible directly from a phone (with a simple verification step).

The UK government is moving to tackle deepfakes by creating a “world-first” evaluation framework to test and standardise deepfake detection tools, working with partners like Microsoft, academics and industry, and aiming to set clear expectations for companies. Alongside fast-tracked laws criminalising the creation or request of non-consensual intimate deepfake images (and plans to target “nudification” tools), the Home Office has launched a Deepfake Detection Challenge with benchmark testing and a live hack event to stress-test detection against real threats such as fraud and impersonation, with broad participation from law enforcement and tech. The effort highlights harms to women and girls, cites a sharp rise in deepfake volume, and comes amid calls from lawmakers to tighten online safety rules and require privacy/safety-by-design so regulators can hold platforms and AI providers accountable

San José has expanded an AI-powered transit signal prioritisation system, built with traffic software provider Lyt, across all city bus routes, reporting a 20% increase in bus speeds. Using real-time traffic data to prioritise green lights for buses at intersections, the system aims to cut delays, improve on-time performance and reduce rider wait times while supporting the city’s congestion and emissions goals. The citywide rollout follows a 2023 pilot on two routes that reduced red-light wait time by 50% and improved reliability, and it fits within San José’s broader push to apply AI for practical services—alongside staff upskilling, safer-streets analytics, streamlined permitting, expanded language access, and initiatives to widen public access to AI tools and education.

A new feature added to the Foster Power app aims to help foster teens who are at higher risk of human trafficking by putting education and support resources directly on their phones. Advocates say instability—made worse by Florida’s shortage of foster homes—can increase vulnerability, especially for teens in “night-to-night” placements. The updated app section explains trafficking and grooming in youth-friendly language, highlights warning signs, and connects teens to help so they can recognize unsafe situations and know support is available, while advocates stress that wider community involvement (more foster homes, mentors, and supportive adults) remains essential.

The Tampa Police Department has rolled out several AI-enabled tools to support officers and 911 dispatchers in time-sensitive incidents, including Prepared 911 and Axon Assistant’s Policy Chat & Translation. Officers’ body-worn cameras can now auto-detect and translate conversations in real time across 54 languages, helping avoid delays when a translator isn’t available, while dispatchers can send a secure link that lets callers share live video or photos during emergencies and communicate via text if they can’t speak. The department is also using an AI policy-search feature that lets officers quickly query procedures during calls, and officials say the tools are meant to assist—not replace—officers, improve speed, safety, and transparency, and are funded through existing contracts and county 911 support.

Lakeland, Florida has signed a four-year contract with Roadways Management Technologies to use “AI Sensor Roadway Intelligence” to monitor pavement conditions and address potholes more quickly. The city will equip 15 municipal vehicles with sensors and cameras that capture images about every 75 feet and measure factors like vehicle vibrations to assess road quality daily, sending the data to a database for analysis. Officials say this real-time approach is more efficient and cheaper than the previous manual survey method done every two years at higher cost, and the system is expected to be ready on March 1.

In Pinellas County, Florida, families can now access a free online child-safety resource through a partnership backed by local law enforcement and funded by the Juvenile Welfare Board, which is covering annual subscriptions to Parent Pro-Tech. The platform provides videos and guides to help parents protect kids from online predators, cyberbullying, and other digital risks by explaining parental controls, social media and AI-related issues, and encouraging parents to ask practical questions about who their children interact with online. Officials say many investigations show parents often don’t realize what’s happening, so the goal is to improve parental awareness and reduce opportunities for predators.

Tampa has signed a three-year contract with One.network to speed up how road and lane closure information reaches drivers through GPS apps. Instead of manually sending updates to platforms like Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Waze—often through emails and spreadsheets—city staff can now enter closures and work-zone changes in One.network and push them to GPS providers within minutes. Officials say the tool should improve real-time coordination around construction impacts and help drivers navigate detours more easily, with the same updates also appearing on the city’s road-closures website.

The European Commission has issued new guidelines to help Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and media providers apply the European Media Freedom Act rules that protect professional journalistic content from unjustified removal online. Under Article 18(1), platforms must give advance notice before taking down journalism, explain the reasons, and allow media providers 24 hours to respond; to access these safeguards, media outlets must submit a declaration (via a platform feature) showing they meet criteria like editorial independence and regulatory oversight. The guidelines explain how platforms should set up and assess these declarations, when to consult regulators, and how civil society groups (including fact-checkers) can be involved, reflecting input from a broad stakeholder consultation and building on the Act’s provisions in force since August 2025.

ICAEW says HMRC has advised that some businesses may now need to enter their VAT registration application reference number when enrolling VAT into their Business Tax Account. HMRC sends this reference number to the email used during VAT registration and includes it on the VAT registration approval letter. HMRC says the change is intended to help prevent fraud, with more details expected in the February 2026 Agent Update.

From 1 February 2026, Poland’s mandatory KSeF e-invoicing will also change VAT reporting because the JPK_VDEK (SAF-T VAT return) schema will require new, mandatory invoice reference data for every invoice: either a KSeF identification number or an approved code (OFF, BFK, or DI) when no KSeF number exists.

SARS is introducing an online registration system for Income Tax Exempt Institutions. This digital system aligns with SARS’s strategic objective to simplify taxpayer compliance through digital platforms.

The pilot will commence on 8 December 2025 until 26 February 2026, and will include the migration and data take-on of all existing records and pilot trade testing. The approach will ensure an improved taxpayer experience once the full system is launched on 27 February 202

Vietnam’s Department of Taxation will pilot an online tax declaration portal later this month to prepare household businesses for a nationwide shift from the old lump-sum system to mandatory digital self-declaration starting Jan. 1, 2026. Officials say the pilot and a 60-day transition campaign will help assess traders’ readiness (devices, software, policy understanding) and provide hands-on support, especially for older market vendors. The rollout is backed by the Ministry of Finance and tech firms offering low-cost tools such as e-invoicing, accounting software and digital signatures, with examples including Sapo’s free “Sapo 6870” package and Viettel’s AI-enabled Tendoo platform, while Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City are running tailored local support programs and the government is drafting new legal and simplified accounting frameworks for household taxpayers.

Singapore banks are phasing out the use of NRIC numbers for authentication after guidance from the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The Association of Banks in Singapore noted that NRIC numbers are not sufficient for financial transactions, which already rely on multi-factor authentication, and most banks have already stopped using NRIC for non-transactional checks such as opening encrypted email attachments. Any remaining uses will be replaced with alternative methods in the coming months, in line with the PDPC’s requirement for organisations to stop using NRIC numbers for authentication by 1 January 2027.

Alabama’s Department of Transportation (ALDOT) is upgrading its performance-based highway maintenance budgeting by using Bentley Systems’ AI-powered Blyncsy to gather more consistent, objective condition data across the state’s roughly 11,000 miles of roads. Instead of relying mainly on labor-intensive manual inspections, Blyncsy analyzes crowdsourced, high-resolution dashcam imagery to automatically assess roadway assets like guardrails and signs, helping ALDOT link real asset conditions to funding decisions. The department says this improves efficiency and consistency, and Bentley notes a prior pilot showed the AI models reaching about 97% accuracy, supporting more precise maintenance planning.

GSA has begun adding new cybersecurity requirements to certain new contracts that resemble the Defense Department’s CMMC approach, focusing on protecting Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) in contractor systems. A Jan. 5 procedural guide from GSA’s Office of the Chief Information Security Officer directs contractors to implement NIST 800-171 (and some 800-172 controls), with “blocker” requirements like multi-factor authentication for all users, encryption of CUI in transit and at rest, vulnerability scanning/remediation, and removing end-of-life components, plus documentation such as security plans and system inventories. Contractors must undergo independent assessments (via FedRAMP third parties or GSA-approved assessors) and follow a five-phase process—prepare, document, assess, authorize, monitor—with ongoing monitoring and periodic reviews; the framework can be applied immediately to new CUI-related contracts at the contracting officer’s discretion, though assessor approval criteria and lists have not been clearly published.

New York State’s Department of State has reopened its Local Government Efficiency Grant program, offering $8 million to help local governments collaborate on projects that streamline services, share resources, or consolidate operations to lower costs and reduce residents’ tax burden. Since 2018, the program has funded 655 projects worth over $121 million, with the state estimating eventual savings of more than $680 million, and the new round prioritises areas like IT and cybersecurity, emergency services, code enforcement, water/wastewater and clean energy. Applications are due in February, with about $7.2 million for implementation grants (up to $250,000 per participating municipality) and $800,000 for planning grants (up to $20,000), plus a one-year $25,000 qualification grant for certain regional initiatives.

The US TSA has added Smiths Detection’s SDX 100100 DV HC X-ray scanner to its Air Cargo Screening Technology List (ACSTL), allowing regulated air-cargo operators to use it under TSA screening standards. The scanner uses dual-view imaging (horizontal and vertical) via two 160 kV X-ray generators to speed inspection of densely packed cargo in a single pass, with options for high or low conveyor configurations and different belt speeds for higher throughput. The article also notes Smiths Detection’s broader role in security screening and that Smiths Group has agreed to sell the division to CVC in a deal expected to close in the second half of 2026, pending regulatory approvals.

Angola has deployed SITA’s API PNR Gateway at Dr. António Agostinho Neto International Airport in Luanda to strengthen border security and modernise border management. The system enables airlines to send Advance Passenger Information (passport/identity details) and Passenger Name Record data (itineraries and bookings) to authorities before departure, giving officials earlier visibility to assess risks and manage migration flows more effectively. The rollout includes a new Passenger Information Monitoring and Management Centre in Luanda, located next to a dedicated data centre for real-time analysis and fast processing, and is intended to align Angola with international security standards while supporting its ambition to become a regional transport hub.

The Northern Territory Government launched QR-code, web-based interactive maps at Territory Wildlife Park and George Brown Darwin Botanic Gardens to help visitors navigate outdoor sites in real time without downloading an app. The maps use geolocation and 30+ languages, can be updated quickly for operational changes, and may provide data to improve visitor flow planning. The rollout will expand to more attractions, including Alice Springs Desert Park in March 2026, with potential future features like educational and accessibility layers.

Nebraska colleges are adopting AI bots to teach practical, ethical AI use rather than banning it. At Doane University, students built “ClubCompass” to guide peers through creating new clubs (rules, constitution, budget, fundraising) and developed other bots for event scheduling and baseball training analysis. At Nebraska Wesleyan University, social work students use an AI bot to simulate group therapy sessions in a controlled setting, practice facilitation skills, and refine language through iterative prompts. Both schools emphasize critical thinking, responsible use, and preparing students for an AI-enabled workforce, with NWU moving toward an AI literacy minor.

Idaho accelerated AI adoption in 2025 to improve resident services and internal efficiency, led by CIO Alberto Gonzalez. The state quickly built an AI governance framework plus training to enable safe use, and is already seeing major productivity gains: in child welfare, a secure language model cut case-review time from 4.5–6 hours to under a minute; at the DMV, AI is being used to automate data entry from handwritten documents and to speed up staff onboarding from months to weeks. Idaho is also linking AI efforts with stronger privacy and ADA focus for 2026, modernizing websites (Idaho.gov expected to relaunch in January), and prioritizing AI chatbots on state sites to help users navigate services. Cybersecurity remains a major priority, including exercises and “Operation Cyber Idaho,” which places cyber interns/apprentices with local governments and schools. The state’s multiyear IT consolidation is nearing completion, with the final agency expected to be consolidated by June.

UK police have launched a six-month pilot of live facial recognition (LFR) at railway stations, starting at London Bridge under the British Transport Police (BTP), with plans to expand to other major London hubs. The system uses NEC’s NeoFace M40 algorithm (evaluated by the National Physical Laboratory) and works by scanning faces against a watchlist of wanted offenders, while deleting non-matches. BTP says it will publish a full evaluation after the pilot.

The article says the FBI is using advanced forensics — especially its Next Generation Identification (NGI) biometric system — to generate leads in the abduction case of 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie in Tucson. Investigators may use facial recognition (NGI-IPS) on available surveillance imagery to produce a ranked list of possible matches (treated as leads, not definitive IDs), and use fingerprint/palm-print searches on recovered physical evidence for stronger identification

Virginia launched SUDA (Substance Use Disorder Analytics), a dashboard that combines overdose, health, 911, public safety, treatment and risk-factor data into one system. It uses tools like heat maps to spot emerging overdose hot spots and quickly compare them with where funding and services are currently allocated, helping officials adjust resources sooner. SUDA also lets users drill into regional/demographic patterns and drug market trends to tailor interventions, aiming to move from reactive reporting to predicting risk and preventing deaths. It was developed by Virginia’s Office of Data Governance and Analytics with state partners, and will expand from state use to local governments, researchers and responders.

A new initiative (FAIR-PReSONS) is developing a bias-free AI system to predict recidivism (reoffending) and help justice systems prioritize rehabilitation interventions more effectively. The project aligns with EU requirements for non-discriminatory AI, recognizing that biased data and variables (e.g., gender, race, nationality) can lead to unfair outcomes.

Jalna police (Maharashtra, India) launched an AI-powered crime and criminal database to speed up FIR and chargesheet processing and improve investigations. The system extracts key details in seconds, auto-fills official reports (including the Daily Crime Report format), cross-checks FIRs against chargesheets to flag discrepancies, and builds detailed offender profiles (photos, history, markings, habits, modus operandi). Officers can search suspects by modus operandi, location, police station, address, and crime history. Police say it has improved accuracy, reduced clerical errors, and helped update 450+ profiles in a month, with plans to expand and integrate across stations.

The European Commission’s ProtectEU roadmap aims to modernize lawful law-enforcement access to digital evidence as crime becomes more digital (about 85% of investigations rely on electronic evidence). It proposes action across six priority areas to make access more consistent, effective and cross-border, while protecting fundamental rights (privacy, data protection, fair trial) and cybersecurity:

AI at scale: Promote AI tools to help filter/analyze huge datasets responsibly, aligned with the EU AI Act.

Data retention: Assess updates to EU rules for retaining non-content data (metadata, location, time) and harmonize approaches after the 2006 directive was invalidated.

Lawful interception: Improve cross-border real-time interception for OTT messaging by 2027, strengthening secure cooperation tools.

Digital forensics: Build technical capacity, fund tools, and support Europol becoming a centre of excellence.

Decryption/encryption: Publish an encryption technology roadmap to identify lawful ways to access encrypted data without undermining security and rights.

Standardisation: Coordinate EU standards for interoperability in forensics, lawful disclosure, and interception.

The roadmap also discusses contested “decryption” approaches: client-side scanning, key escrow, security gateways/“ghost users”, and lawful device access (government hacking)—each with major trade-offs in legality, privacy, oversight, and cybersecurity risk

Tarrant County commissioners approved an agreement allowing the Sheriff’s Office to use two AI tools (Gracie and Transaction Intercept) from the nonprofit Street Grace (backed by Microsoft) to support investigations into online child exploitation. The tools analyze publicly available online data to flag patterns and help investigators handle large volumes of information, but officials say AI is only an investigative aid and must be verified with traditional evidence.

EPA has published a final rule titled “Rescission of the Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and Motor Vehicle Greenhouse Gas Emission Standards Under the Clean Air Act” that rescinds the 2009 GHG Endangerment Finding and repeals the federal GHG emission standards for new motor vehicles and engines across multiple EPA vehicle rules (40 CFR parts 85, 86, 600, 1036, 1037, 1039). The rule was published Feb 18, 2026 (Document No. 2026-03157; 91 FR 7686) and is scheduled to be effective April 20, 2026, framing the change as a major shift in how EPA uses Clean Air Act authority for vehicle GHG regulation.

South Africa’s tax authority (SARS) confirmed a phased, multi-year reform to introduce mandatory e-invoicing and real-time (or near real-time) VAT digital reporting. Strategic SARS publications (2022–2025) position e-invoicing as a core pillar of VAT modernization to reduce the VAT gap, curb fraud/refund abuse, and shift VAT from declaration-based reporting to transaction-level data driven compliance — aligned with the vision to “make tax just happen.”

A project (Feb 2025–Sep 2026) is testing a machine-learning model to predict import tax evasion and reduce customs corruption in low- and middle-income countries. Using a randomized controlled trial in Paraguay, it evaluates whether the algorithm can improve targeting accuracy, cut inspection delays, and ultimately strengthen state capacity and increase tax revenue.

Italy’s tax authority (Agenzia delle Entrate) is using AI to speed up VAT refunds and improve fraud detection, but only in the pre-assessment screening stage — humans still make final decisions. VAT data from e-invoices, cross-border reports, customs declarations, and banking/withholding sources is cleaned and cross-checked, then refund claims are risk-scored using pattern recognition, network analysis, historical profiles and text analysis. Early trials are promising: by Sept 2025 the average refund time dropped to 67 days (beating the 70-day 2025 target), and Italy expects automatic processing for low-risk refunds by 2026. The agency also stresses a privacy-cautious approach, avoiding scraping online/social media data.
The U.S. Treasury (Bureau of the Fiscal Service) is looking to expand data access for its Do Not Pay system to help agencies detect fraud before payments go out

Boston’s Office of Emerging Technology and city partners have launched the Boston Curb (Kerb) Lab to build a real-time, AI-powered “digital understanding” of parking regulations and kerb space so residents can quickly answer “can I park here?” and the city can balance competing demands like parking, loading, deliveries and safety. Using modern data tools, the lab aims to connect previously disconnected curb datasets (built up over decades) into a citywide map of parking rules and to develop practical tools already underway such as reliable tow-zone alerts, tracking food-delivery congestion and safety impacts, and publishing public maps that improve parking accessibility—supporting wider goals like Go Boston 2030 and Vision Zero.

geoRoad.ai, a Malaysia-based company, is piloting an AI-driven road infrastructure platform across 20+ road networks in Malaysia, Spain, the UK, Mexico and Italy, using AI, edge computing, and real-time video/sensor analysis to spot hazards like potholes, cracks, water ponding, stray animals and road debris before they cause harm—helping municipalities streamline hazard reporting, prioritize high-risk areas, reduce maintenance workload, and shift from reactive repairs to proactive road safety management

On Feb. 12, 2026, California’s Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) issued an Imminent and Substantial Endangerment and Remedial Action Order to Magellan Aerospace, Middletown, Inc., and Market Creek Plaza LLC to require an immediate cleanup of trichloroethylene (TCE) contamination near the former Fleet Aerospace Langley Facility in San Diego after testing found elevated TCE in indoor air and soil vapor at Market Creek Plaza and a nearby residential complex, with indoor-air levels reported up to eight times the health screening level. DTSC says TCE — historically used in aerospace manufacturing — can enter buildings through “vapor intrusion” (through foundation cracks) and is associated with serious health risks, including cancer and reproductive harm; the order requires rapid vapor mitigation at residences (e.g., air treatment/ventilation improvements), continued indoor-air sampling, investigation and cleanup of contaminated soil/soil vapor/groundwater, and actions to stop further migration. DTSC warned that noncompliance can trigger penalties up to $25,000 per day and noted Magellan has 15 days to respond and begin cleanup, while DTSC coordinates with local agencies and oversees protections for workers and residents (including at the Euclid Apartments).

California’s Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) announced it has completed a major cleanup milestone at the former Rocketdyne-Atomics International Rifle and Pistol Club Shooting Range and Overshot Area (the “Former Shooting Range”) on the 31-acre Sage Ranch property in Ventura County, a sensitive wildlife corridor with public trails. Under an Imminent and Substantial Endangerment Determination and Consent (IS&E) Order and a 2022 agreement naming Boeing as the responsible party, DTSC oversaw a time-critical removal action that ran from June 2023 to January 2025 to address soil contamination from historic recreational shooting, primarily lead particles and shot (plus arsenic, antimony, and PAHs linked to clay targets). About 27,500 cubic yards of contaminated soil were excavated and disposed of offsite, with dust, worker exposure, and stormwater controls used throughout; DTSC approved the Final Removal Action Completion Report in November 2025. While remediation is complete, habitat restoration and revegetation continue, the trail segment crossing the area is expected to remain closed for about three years, and Boeing will conduct a one-year restoration/soil stabilization review in November 2026, as part of the wider cleanup of the 2,849-acre Santa Susana Field Laboratory site involving Boeing, NASA, and DOE.

Viet Nam’s Ministry of Justice, with FPT as technology partner, has rolled out the Civil Judgment Enforcement (CJE) Digital Platform nationwide as a major justice-sector digital transformation, driven by a 2025 workload of 1,063,030 enforcement cases worth VND 683.8 trillion, a restructuring from 63 to 34 provincial authorities, and amended civil judgment enforcement legislation that made digitalisation mandatory with some provisions effective from Jan 20, 2026. The platform went live systemwide on Jan 20, 2026 across 34 provincial authorities and 355 regional offices serving 6,800+ users, with four core modules (e-receipts, decision support, enforcement operations, and complaints/denunciations) digitising 100% of professional processes and citizen interactions; early results include 100% of enforcement decisions issued electronically via an AI-integrated system, 600,000+ e-receipts replacing paper for transactions over VND 30 trillion, ~30% faster processing, up to 80% fewer administrative steps, stronger real-time oversight to reduce misconduct “gray areas,” plus local leadership such as Ho Chi Minh City’s first CJE Intelligent Operations Center and Hanoi’s pilot for citizen reception and complaint handling, built on FPT’s Make-in-Viet Nam Kyta Platform (AI + low-code + high integration).

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey announced the creation of the Technology Quality Assurance Board (TQAB) to guide the responsible, secure and effective use of AI and other emerging technologies across state executive agencies, with a strong focus on cybersecurity, privacy and operational standards.

Malaysia’s Ministry of Transport is moving toward a data-driven road enforcement model that reduces reliance on disruptive physical roadblocks, which often cause congestion at highway exits and toll areas, by expanding Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) and integrating it with government vehicle and driver databases. With networked cameras and real-time plate recognition, authorities could verify road tax, insurance and registration without stopping traffic, flag non-compliant or stolen vehicles, and trigger near real-time alerts for targeted follow-up—shifting enforcement from manual, location-bound checks to intelligence-led operations. Success depends on interoperable systems, secure cross-agency data sharing and accurate data, while the same aggregated movement data can also improve traffic management, safety analysis and evidence-based policy, with human staff refocused on investigation and higher-value interventions.

INRIX is partnering with the Ohio and Pennsylvania departments of transportation to provide real-time traffic data (such as vehicle speeds, signal analytics and bottlenecks) that helps agencies analyze how drivers move and improve efficiency and safety. Ohio DOT feeds multiple INRIX data points into its TOAST tool to rank major corridors and support TSMO decisions, including evaluating winter road treatment by tracking when speeds return to normal after snow/ice events. PennDOT uses INRIX real-time and historical speed data to design and operate a “queue protection system” on 23 corridors (about 1,150 miles), automatically triggering dynamic message signs when speed thresholds indicate slow or stopped traffic and updating queue distance every minute; INRIX reports these warnings have reduced crashes by 11% overall and fatal truck crashes by 46%.

The text explains how NIST-led initiatives are boosting first responders’ safety by improving indoor situational awareness where GPS and standard drone navigation struggle: a NIST prize challenge pushes drones to generate usable, high-quality 3D indoor maps of complex, hazardous buildings so commanders can identify obstacles and potential victims and plan safer routes, while the First Responder Smart Tracking (FRST) Challenge seeks rugged, affordable wearable localization systems that track responders inside multi-story structures in near real time. It also highlights NIST’s new Public Safety Immersive Test Center in Colorado, a modular facility that recreates disaster scenarios (collapsed structures, smoke-filled interiors, multi-agency responses) to test drone mapping, indoor tracking and communications together, aiming to make these tools reliable and interoperable—augmenting human teams and helping save lives.

South Korea has launched a three-year, ₩13.2 billion (about $9.8 million) project to build a monitoring system targeting drug trafficking that uses cryptocurrencies on the dark web and other anonymous channels. Led by the Ministry of Science and ICT with the National Police Agency, the system is expected to analyze patterns across anonymous networks to identify who is behind drug-sale posts, track suspicious flows of illegal funds linked to crypto transactions, and use AI to automatically collect and update the slang and coded phrases used in drug advertisements. Officials say advanced analytics are needed to keep up with evolving tactics that exploit platforms like the dark web and Telegram.

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Finance launched a voluntary pilot on Feb. 2, 2026 allowing public procurement suppliers to pay VAT using the digital tenge (the country’s digital currency), running until Dec. 31, 2026. Participating suppliers must apply through a second-tier bank to open a digital-tenge account, sign a data-exchange agreement with the state revenue authority, and confirm VAT payments in digital tenge. The system “marks” the VAT portion of each payment, and those marked funds can only be used to pay VAT to the state budget or to transfer VAT under an electronic VAT invoice to another VAT payer, while any unmarked digital tenge can be converted back to a regular bank account.

CIAT and Alagoas’ finance secretariat (SEFAZ-AL) held Phase 2 technical meetings to advance the SATI Integrated Tax Administration System, aligning governance and quality protocols to build a new digital ecosystem that will gradually replace legacy platforms. CIAT presented a Governance and Quality Plan using agile methods and international QA standards, while teams set roadmaps for key products (like public policy evaluation and management control), introduced real-time project monitoring tools (Jira and Xray) for transparent milestone tracking, and launched integration work across legal affairs, active debt and revenue collection to reduce information silos. The project aims to modernize tax administration, improve efficiency, cut operating costs and strengthen taxpayer relations through more robust and transparent systems.

CIAT, with support from GIZ and EUROsociAL+, has completed publishing the full Manual for the Control of International Tax Planning, developed over more than three years by 55 experts from CIAT’s International Taxation Network. The manual consists of 42 sections that help tax administrations understand key international tax risks (including harmful planning behaviors like transfer pricing manipulation, treaty abuse, hybrids, profit shifting and digital-economy risks), and provides legal/administrative containment measures (GAAR/SAAR, anti-hybrid and transparency rules, transfer pricing regulations, tax-haven measures, promoter disclosure, PE/commissionaire abuse controls) plus practical tools (information regimes and databases, international cooperation, cooperative compliance, crypto taxation and APAs). Two sections—on risk-identification mechanisms and audits of multinationals—are restricted to tax administration officials and available only upon request via CIAT’s email, and CIAT credits multiple partner institutions (e.g., AEAT, OECD, IRS and others) for enabling the initiative.

CIAT, supported by GIZ and COSEFIN, published the Taxation and Gender Study, the first regional analysis based on official tax records disaggregated by gender. The study urges tax administrations to embed a gender perspective across their work — especially in strategic planning, data production and analysis, audit processes, and coordination with other state institutions. Using gender-disaggregated records from the tax administrations of 11 countries, it examines gender gaps across key tax areas, including Personal Income Tax (PIT), Value Added Tax (VAT) and Wealth Tax. The publication is positioned as an innovative tool that provides evidence and recommendations to help tax administrations advance substantive gender equality and build fairer tax systems.

Ho Chi Minh City is emerging as a major hub for billion-dollar data centre investments fueled by rapid AI adoption and Vietnam’s push to expand digital infrastructure, prompting the city to form an inter-agency task force to speed approvals and remove red tape. Projects include a flagship AI-focused hyperscale facility estimated at US$2 billion on 10 hectares in Tan Phu Trung Industrial Park, plus other large builds such as a 140 MW Tier III centre with about 10,000 racks and up to 60 kW rack density, a Saigon Hi-Tech Park hyperscale site with 30 MW IT load and 3,000 racks rolling out in phases from 2026–2030 (construction Q2 2026, operations Q2 2027), and another campus backed by US$500 million. The boom aligns with global projections of near-doubling data-centre capacity to 200 GW by 2030 and massive investment needs, while Vietnam’s attractiveness is strengthened by power planning, renewables, high internet use, government support and low construction costs (around US$7 per watt), positioning Ho Chi Minh City as a key growth centre despite Vietnam’s current operational capacity of roughly 104 MW.

Illinois House Bill 4224, introduced by Rep. Kimberly Du Buclet, would create a program allowing some state prison inmates to take remote jobs with approved participating businesses, with pay deposited directly into their Illinois Department of Corrections accounts. To qualify, inmates would need basics like a high school diploma (or exemption), at least 30 days served at the facility, general-population status, participation in education/vocational programs, recent good disciplinary standing, and eligibility to use a computer and internet under IDOC rules. The bill also sets exclusions for people with computer-related offenses or restrictions, and bans work involving sensitive data (like HIPAA-protected info or Illinois criminal justice data), with the program slated to take effect Jan. 1, 2027 if signed into law.

County leaders from 15 states urged Congress to pass the FEMA Act, a bill aimed at speeding disaster recovery and improving transparency by simplifying aid for survivors, accelerating infrastructure repairs and reforming FEMA processes. The legislation would create a universal disaster application to cut paperwork and delays, and a public tracking website showing project approvals and payments. It also proposes changes to FEMA’s Public Assistance program to allow faster, grant-based funding and would cover certain loan interest costs local governments incur while responding. Advocates say counties helped shape the reforms, and they point to the growing scale of disasters—more than a third of U.S. counties saw at least one federally declared disaster in 2023.

The NIH launched its Biosafety Modernization Initiative on Sept. 9, 2025 to build a “21st-century” biosafety framework that matches today’s faster, more multidisciplinary biomedical research, aiming for risk-based oversight beyond recombinant DNA/synthetic nucleic acids (potentially covering wild-type agents, toxins/prions and infectious microbes) while reducing oversight for historically low-risk work, aligning with CDC/NIH BMBL guidance, and excluding areas already regulated by FDA/USDA/EPA. A key focus is strengthening Institutional Biosafety Committees (IBCs) with resources comparable to IRBs and IACUCs. The initiative follows a four-phase timeline: Phase I (Fall 2025) listening sessions and outreach; Phase II (Winter 2025–Spring 2026) synthesize input and publish a draft for public comment; Phase III (Spring–Summer 2026) refine the draft and assess guidance needs; and Phase IV (Fall 2026) release the final policy with guidance plus education and outreach, with ongoing public feedback accepted via email/NIH portal.

The Land Bank of the Philippines launched its Cash-Lite Campus Programme at the State University of Northern Negros to give 2,000+ students and campus partners secure digital banking for tuition, meals and other on-campus payments, while also strengthening financial literacy through practical tools for budgeting, saving and safe spending. LANDBANK helped students open no-deposit, no-minimum PISO Plus accounts via its mobile app, trained them on account security and QR person-to-merchant payments, and expects higher digital transaction use building on SUNN’s earlier Link.BizPortal adoption (1,000+ transactions worth nearly ₱1.5 million by 2025). The initiative is part of a nationwide push for youth financial inclusion, with nearly 10,000 participants so far and additional rollouts across other Philippine campuses, including a February 2026 launch at Metro Dumaguete College as the first fully cash-lite campus in the Visayas.

Malaysia is modernising border management by rolling out automated e-gates and biometric screening nationwide, aiming for full implementation by 2028 across Immigration, Customs, Quarantine and Security complexes under the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency. The plan includes installing 635 automated gates at 125 official entry points, using biometrics (including facial recognition and an Automated Biometric Identification System) and automated document checks to speed up and standardise identity verification, while keeping manual counters as backup for continuity. Automation is expected to free immigration officers for higher-risk enforcement and investigations, strengthen security at gazetted crossings to deter document misuse, and improve transparency through clearer audit trails and compliance monitoring. Resilience is built in via offline/independent operation supported by local and central servers, alongside governance measures such as asset declarations and integrity oversight to address human-related risks as the digital system scales.

حصلت جامعة هونغ كونغ بوليتكنيك على 18.6 مليون دولار هونغ كونغي من صندوق المرور الذكي (الدفعة 23) لتمويل ثلاثة مشاريع بحثية تعتمد على الذكاء الاصطناعي والحساسات: تطوير نظام قيادة ذكي متكامل لأساطيل الخدمات اللوجستية يعتمد على دمج حساسات متعددة وإدراك “منظور عين الطائر” بزاوية 360° مع تدريب/تحقق من المحاكاة إلى الواقع وفق شبكة طرق هونغ كونغ؛ ونظام لمراقبة انتباه السائق باستخدام أجهزة قابلة للارتداء يجمع مؤشرات فسيولوجية من أساور ذكية ويحللها بتعلم الآلة لإنتاج مؤشر موحد لفقدان الانتباه وإرسال تنبيهات متدرجة للسائقين ومديري الأسطول؛ ودراسة لتطوير/تكييف نظام كبح طارئ تلقائي للحافلات يتناسب مع ظروف الطرق المحلية عبر تحليل سجلات الحوادث وبيانات المسار الفعلية في اختبارات ظل، مع مراعاة سلامة الركاب. وتهدف هذه المبادرات إلى رفع الكفاءة والسلامة المرورية في بيئة حضرية كثيفة، ضمن مسار استثماري أوسع ارتبط حتى الآن بـ 31 مشروعًا مدعومًا من الصندوق لدى الجامعة.

تُجري منطقة تعليمية في مينيسوتا (Southwest Metro Intermediate District 288) تجربة مبكرة لنظام ملاحظة صفّية مدعوم بالذكاء الاصطناعي باسم Evelyn يقوم بتحليل تسجيلات صوتية ومرئية للدروس (عبر كاميرا صفّية بزاوية 360 درجة) لإنتاج ملاحظات مُؤطّرة وفق معايير تقييم مرتبطة بإطار Danielson وبشكل مُفصّل مع طوابع زمنية، بهدف تسريع التغذية الراجعة للمعلمين وتقليل عبء الإداريين. وتقول الإدارة إن ارتفاع نسبة المعلمين الجدد ومتطلبات الملاحظات السنوية خلقا “عنق زجاجة” في التدريب، وإن نتائج المقارنة الأولية بين تقييمات النظام وتقييمات إداريين مدرَّبين كانت متقاربة جدًا في المتوسط، مع رصد مشكلات مثل تشدد التقييم في بعض صفوف التربية الخاصة قبل ضبط النظام لاحتساب التكييفات التعليمية. كما أثارت التجربة أسئلة الخصوصية والمراقبة، لذلك يجري العمل بمشورة قانونية وتُعامل الفيديوهات كسجلات تعليمية محمية، مع التأكيد أن الهدف هو دعم المُقيّمين البشر لا استبدالهم.

أطلقت الأمم المتحدة بوابة التعاون الرقمي في 4 ديسمبر 2025 لدعم تنفيذ الميثاق الرقمي العالمي عبر تجميع مبادرات التعاون الرقمي حول العالم في منصة واحدة تشمل مجالات مثل الاقتصاد الرقمي الشامل، حوكمة الذكاء الاصطناعي، البنية التحتية الرقمية، وحماية حقوق الإنسان على الإنترنت. طُوّرت البوابة بواسطة مكتب الأمم المتحدة للتقنيات الرقمية والناشئة (ODET) وبمساهمات من الأونكتاد (UNCTAD) واليونيدو (UNIDO)، وتستخدم أدوات مدعومة بالذكاء الاصطناعي لربط المبادرات المتشابهة واقتراح فرص للتعاون وتتبع التطورات بشكل شبه فوري، بما يعزز الشفافية والشمولية وكفاءة التنسيق. كما أنها متاحة عالميًا للدول الأعضاء ووكالات الأمم المتحدة والمجتمع المدني والباحثين والشركات لإضافة المعلومات ومشاركة المبادرات.

توسّع ولاية كولورادو برنامجًا تجريبيًا للإتاحة عبر توفير جلسة ترجمة فورية بلغة الإشارة الأمريكية (ASL) لمدة 30 دقيقة مجانًا لزوار مبنى الكابيتول باستخدام تطبيق Aira ASL الذي يربط المستخدم بمترجم محترف يمكنه الاستعانة بكاميرا الهاتف للمساعدة في الترجمة لحظيًا. ويأتي التمويل عبر برنامج الإتاحة التقنية في مكتب تقنية المعلومات بالولاية، كما تتوفر الخدمة في 32 موقعًا للتأهيل المهني و46 مركزًا للقوى العاملة و11 متحفًا وموقعًا تاريخيًا، وذلك امتدادًا لتجربة Aira Explorer التي بدأت عام 2023 لدعم المكفوفين وضعاف البصر في التنقل داخل المباني. وتؤكد الولاية أن التوسعة تعزز الخدمات العادلة والميسّرة للجميع وتدعم مشاركة مجتمع الصم في العملية التشريعية.

California has launched Poppy, a secure, state-built generative AI assistant that only California state employees can use; it runs entirely on state networks and pulls information only from official CA.gov websites so prompts, documents and responses don’t leave the government environment. Started as a pilot in September under Gov. Newsom’s 2023 AI executive order, Poppy already has 2,600+ users across 66 departments, is free during the pilot but capped at 100 users per agency, and is being used for tasks like policy analysis, succession planning and form completion, while flagging/redacting or refusing requests involving PII (e.g., Social Security numbers) to support privacy, fairness and security; after the pilot ends in June, the state plans to expand access and strengthen user training so staff set realistic expectations and use it responsibly.

India has strengthened its anti-narcotics governance through the NCORD mechanism, an institutional platform linking central ministries, state governments and enforcement agencies to coordinate monitoring of drug trafficking, precursor diversion, demand reduction and rehabilitation

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz unveiled a broad anti-fraud legislative package to strengthen oversight of state social safety-net programs, with a key focus on using predictive analytics and machine learning to flag suspicious transactions and billing earlier in the application process.

Dublin City Council hosted Ireland’s first government use case for quantum-secure communications by trialling advanced encryption over its existing municipal fibre network to help protect public services from future cyber threats. The demonstration is part of IrelandQCI, a €10 million programme co-funded by the European Commission and Ireland’s Department of Culture, Communications and Sport, and it contributes to the wider EuroQCI initiative to roll out secure quantum communications across Europe.

New joint guidance from the UK’s Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) and HM Treasury confirms that regulated firms can use certified Digital Verification Services (DVS) to meet Money Laundering Regulations customer due diligence (CDD) requirements, helping them move from manual document checks to secure digital onboarding. It ties compliance to the government’s digital identity and attributes trust framework, stressing that firms should rely on providers listed on the official DVS Register (and that non-listed services should not be treated as reliably compliant). The guidance clarifies that digital ID can support identity verification for individuals and company directors, but firms remain fully responsible for end-to-end AML duties, including risk assessment, enhanced due diligence for high-risk cases, understanding the business relationship, and recordkeeping. The government estimates broad digital ID adoption could add £701m per year to the UK economy, and signals potential future consultation on a state-issued Digital ID.

The Philippines’ Bureau of Internal Revenue launched its 2026 national tax campaign, highlighting a shift to digital-first enforcement and taxpayer services after a record ₱3.105 trillion collection in 2025 (helped by the Estate Tax Amnesty, which raised ₱4.603 billion from 100,000+ participants). The 2026 agenda focuses on expanding digital tools to reduce leakages and simplify compliance, building on the fact that e-payments made up 85% of 2025 collections. New measures include an interactive digital tax calendar, a QR-based “Registration Seal Badge” now mandatory for e-commerce/online businesses to verify legitimacy, and a ChatBot (REVIE) feature that lets taxpayers confirm the authenticity of audit authorizations and field officers in real time to prevent unauthorized audits.

The Philippines’ BIR, Bureau of the Treasury and UnionBank signed an MOA to integrate UnionBank’s UPay facility into the national collection system, expanding web and mobile channels for paying taxes and other government obligations. The deal aims to improve convenience, security, transparency and efficiency in e-payments, ensure timely remittances and accurate records, and consolidates prior agreements for UnionBank’s role as an Authorized Agent Bank for internal revenue taxes and customs duties. Officials said UPay will reduce in-person queues by supporting multiple payment options, including branch payments and digital rails like InstaPay and PayGate, helping strengthen taxpayer trust and voluntary compliance.

Romania’s tax authority ANAF launched “ANA,” an AI chatbot that helps taxpayers quickly get general guidance on tax obligations. It is being piloted first inside users’ Private Virtual Space (SPV) accounts and will later be available on ANAF’s website. The chatbot is part of ANAF’s broader digitalisation programme funded through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, aiming to modernise remote services, reduce administrative burden, and support voluntary compliance. At launch, ANA covers limited topics—initially general obligations for individuals earning income from rentals and/or independent activities—but ANAF says it will be continuously updated and improved through user interactions and feedback, gradually expanding to more tax areas.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) is launching a five-year contact-centre transformation project (RISE) to replace its ageing Genesys Engage platform (in place since 1999) by December 2028, aiming to handle up to 20 million yearly interactions more efficiently. The new system is expected to support voice, chat and self-service at very high volumes, and the ATO is exploring AI—particularly configurable machine learning and large language models—with capabilities like prompt chaining, guardrails, and self-correction, under human oversight and aligned with security, privacy and ethical-use requirements. The ATO also sets strict rules that its data cannot be used to train external AI models, and it is considering whether to replace its current virtual assistant “Alex” as part of the broader modernisation.

North Dakota launched two new online platforms — a Campaign Finance Reporting system and a Statement of Interests portal — to modernize how campaign finance and ethics disclosures are filed and viewed, making contribution/expenditure data and officials’ financial-interest disclosures easier for the public to access. The tools replace older systems with a more user-friendly interface, aim to simplify reporting for candidates and committees that must file under state thresholds, and support transparency by helping voters spot potential conflicts of interest among elected officials and governor-appointed board members. The Secretary of State’s office also plans a virtual demo of the systems on Jan. 26, and the update aligns North Dakota with other states that have recently expanded digital disclosure tools to improve public access to political and ethics records.

China issued new guidelines to use AI in public tendering and bidding to detect corruption and “backroom deals,” as its anti-graft campaign intensifies. The guidance (from the National Development and Reform Commission and other agencies) calls for AI tools to flag irregularities in bid documents, monitor and scrutinize tender review committees’ decisions, and generate recommendations using “human-like” reasoning, while also mining data for clues of bid-rigging to support disciplinary and law-enforcement authorities. Reuters notes AI has already been used in practice: in Zhejiang, an official was detained after AI flagged suspicious patterns in multiple projects’ tenders; state media said he took bribes and helped channel payoffs to reviewers, and he was later sentenced to 2.5 years in prison.

Norway’s $2.2 trillion sovereign wealth fund (NBIM) is using AI — including large language models — to screen newly added companies for ESG-related risks such as links to forced labour, corruption, fraud and other controversies. Since 2025, the system scans public information (often missed by commercial data vendors, especially for smaller firms in emerging markets and in local-language media) within 24 hours of an investment, flags potential issues, and has in some cases enabled NBIM to sell positions before the wider market reacted, helping it avoid losses.

In a January 22, 2026 announcement, the U.S. Department of Commerce said SelectUSA facilitated a record $139 billion in foreign direct investment in the first year of the Trump Administration, covering 175 deals projected to support 32,000+ U.S. jobs across sectors such as ICT, semiconductors, industrial materials, marine tech, healthcare and agriculture; the release also highlights a new public County Cluster Mapping Dashboard that lets companies explore industry clusters at state and county levels using over a million data points, and notes the 2025 SelectUSA Investment Summit drew 5,500+ participants including 2,700+ investors from 100+ countries, with the next summit set for May 3–6, 2026.

Hawaii’s State Archives finished digitizing 64 volumes of historical state records and published them online for free, including scans related to genealogy, land ownership and court proceedings. Started in 2020, the project covers records from the early 1800s to the late 1990s and adds a searchable index to help the public find where needed documents may be located. Officials say the site is a starting point (not a full replacement for in-person research), but it significantly expands access for residents on other islands and researchers outside Hawaii by letting them search anytime and prepare citations before working with archivists.

IIT Gandhinagar has launched the AI Resilience and Command (ARC) Centre to support anticipatory, data-driven climate risk management, with an initial focus on real-time flood assessment for Indian cities. The centre aims to help urban authorities respond faster to extreme events, reduce disruption to mobility and infrastructure, and improve planning, especially as rainfall patterns increasingly trigger short-duration, high-intensity flooding.

This Horizon Europe Cluster 4 call (HORIZON-CL4-2026-04-DIGITAL-EMERGING-09) funds projects to enhance Local Digital Twins with advanced AI to improve early warning and preparedness for flooding, combining high-resolution data (terrain, land use, infrastructure, soil, real-time weather) with hydrological/hydraulic models to run simulations, identify risk areas, and estimate impacts/damage; it emphasizes open, reusable (as open-source as possible) and interoperable solutions aligned with initiatives like Destination Earth and the Global Flood Awareness System, recommending frugal/local AI and aiming to move from TRL 5 to TRL 7. The call opens 15 Jan 2026 and closes 15 Apr 2026 (17:00), with a €6,000,000 call budget (about €6,000,000 per project) and 70% funding rate (NPOs 100%).

Madurai Corporation is installing AI-powered cameras at about 60 locations to stop dumper bins from overflowing. The cameras detect when bins are full or nearly full and automatically alert the local sanitary inspector via an app; if the bin isn’t cleared within 30 minutes, the alert escalates up the chain, and if there’s still no action after 3–4 hours, the commissioner is notified. A command centre will monitor the data, add extra bins in high-waste areas, and the city is also exploring using the system to detect illegal dumping and issue fines

On 26 Feb 2026, the UK government announced it will set up new “blitz” courts to help tackle the criminal case backlog by grouping similar cases into short, intensive hearing periods—starting in London with a focus on assaults on emergency workers—to concentrate expertise, encourage earlier guilty pleas and reduce wasted court time when cases collapse late. Deputy Prime Minister and Justice Secretary David Lammy said the plan sits alongside a three-year funding deal (including £2.78bn for courts and tribunals in 2026–27, up from £2.54bn last year), no cap on Crown Court sitting days, and funding magistrates’ courts to “highest operational capacity,” plus a new National Listing Framework to standardise scheduling, expanded use of AI for transcription (including immigration and asylum tribunals), anonymisation and judgment summaries, a pilot AI-assisted listing tool, more case co-ordinators, and operational changes like allowing prison vans to use bus lanes in some areas.

The UK government plans to amend the Crime and Policing Bill to require tech platforms to remove non-consensual intimate images within 48 hours of being reported, with penalties for noncompliance including fines of up to 10% of global revenue or potential service blocking in the UK.

India’s Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) plans to launch a unified online portal (“CAG-Connect”) in November 2025 so nearly 1 million audited entities can respond digitally to audit queries, observations and inspection reports, as part of a broader shift toward remote and hybrid audits that use risk-based planning, secure access to government platforms (e.g., IFMS, e-procurement) and geospatial tools like PM GatiShakti to expand coverage, reduce on-site time and speed resolution; CAG is also developing an internal CAG-LLM to help auditors analyze large datasets and past reports to spot patterns and improve audit quality

The U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) announced full implementation of Transactional Data Reporting (TDR) across the Multiple Award Schedule, expanding mandatory reporting that started in 2025 and reportedly produced $20.2 million in annual cost avoidance; GSA projects this could reach about $50 million annually once fully established. TDR collects more complete price-and-purchase data to help contracting officers compare prices, negotiate better terms, and make “smarter buying” decisions, while reducing administrative burden versus traditional sales reporting and making it easier for small businesses to participate; the announcement frames TDR as aligned with President Trump’s procurement-consolidation executive order and similar to private-sector data-driven purchasing.

Malaysia is accelerating border modernisation by rolling out automated e-gates and expanded biometric verification nationwide, aiming to install 635 automatic gates across 125 entry points by 2028 under the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency (AKPS) at ICQS complexes. The plan will expand facial recognition and the Automated Biometric Identification System, reduce reliance on manual checks, and redeploy immigration staff to higher-value enforcement and investigations, while keeping staffed counters as backups during outages. Upgrades include stronger local and central server infrastructure and new deployments at key crossings (including Johor Bahru, with additional eGate units and QR scanners), alongside tighter digital identity controls such as requiring Malaysians to authenticate via MyDigital ID to use the MyNIISe mobile app for departures (effective Jan 15). The move also aligns with wider regional biometrics adoption, with nearby Singapore expanding passport-less clearance and trials like facial biometric use for motorcyclists at Woodlands.

CBP’s Intelligence Reporting System–Next Generation (IRS-NG) is a real, documented intelligence platform that can turn routine encounters — including photos, notes, and open-source/social media context — into long-retained intelligence reports that can be shared across DHS via the Analytical Framework for Intelligence (AFI). Built on CBP’s Automated Targeting System (ATS), IRS-NG lets analysts link people, vehicles, locations and events, and even run photos through facial-comparison workflows available through ATS, then publish supervisor-approved intelligence products. Because “relevance” is defined broadly (border security, immigration enforcement, national security, public safety), people who are not accused of crimes — such as legal observers or protesters — can still appear in intelligence products, which the piece says raises First Amendment and “mission creep” concerns. It highlights long retention periods (up to decades), possible errors from static snapshots or unreliable commercial/open-source data, limited notice to individuals, and reports that protest activity has been labeled “domestic terrorism” in internal DHS records; it also notes Sen. Ed Markey seeking clarification on whether DHS is cataloging protesters.

Minnesota is using AI to fight AI-enabled fraud in its Medicaid and social services programs after scammers used tools like ChatGPT to generate fake client notes, emails and documentation to bill for services that never happened; state officials (including Minnesota IT and human services leaders) are deploying machine learning analytics—including work with Optum—to sift through thousands of provider claims and flag suspicious patterns (e.g., impossible volumes of daily client meetings or repeated billing for the same hours), while emphasizing that AI flags are leads, not proof, requiring human investigation and safeguards to reduce false positives; the push is reinforced by Gov. Tim Walz’s proposed anti-fraud package to expand predictive analytics, amid investigations and prosecutions where estimated fraud exposure has been debated and concerns remain about algorithmic errors and the need for fair appeal processes.

The article argues that “digital curb management” — real-time dynamic loading zones, live parking availability and cross-platform coordination — is often more aspirational than immediately achievable because curbs serve many competing users (drivers, delivery fleets, micromobility, city operations), generate complex data needs, and require costly integration and governance; experts say the practical first step is building a single, accurate digital curb map/inventory (a “source of truth”) that is kept up to date as soon as signage or rules change, as Boston’s Curb Lab is doing by using AI to read street signs and translate them into standardized curb data that can be shared across departments and with the public, while cities should stay policy-led (define goals like reducing congestion) and only collect/maintain the specific data they need rather than trying to digitize everything at once.

Government agencies and NGOs in the Philippines are stepping up child protection by combining digital literacy, parental guidance and justice-sector reforms to tackle online and offline abuse, especially OSAEC; advocates warn that perpetrators are using AI to generate explicit child imagery and spread harmful content, but stress that AI-generated sexual images of minors remain illegal under existing OSAEC laws, while programs like World Vision and Lingap Pangkabataan’s CLEAR-CAR campaign equip communities with awareness materials and safer online practices, and in Samar the new Tri-City Justice Zone in Calbayog (under the Justice Sector Coordinating Council) aims to move beyond symbolism by improving coordination among courts, prosecutors, police, corrections and LGUs to speed up child-sensitive case handling, reduce delays and strengthen protection, prevention and prosecution through a more proactive, integrated local justice response.

In Parañaque City, the local government has introduced City Ordinance No. 2025‑30 (69), aimed at enhancing security in public areas through preventive measures supported by technology and community enforcement

Minister of State Rahayu Mahzam launched Phase 2 of TOUCH Community Services’ First Device Campaign, emphasizing that digital-age parenting is harder because children are “digital natives” and many parents face time and skills gaps, so support must move from generic advice to practical, community-based help. She highlighted neighbourhood-level programmes that build peer learning and confidence, plus closer coordination with government agencies to extend resources and partnerships. Framing tech as a necessary part of life rather than an inherent threat, she urged parents to engage, share feedback and learn together to guide children toward meaningful, responsible use. TOUCH Cyber Wellness, a pioneer in cyber wellness and media literacy, supports this through evidence-based education, prevention and intervention programmes, Cyber Wellness Centres and specialised counselling (including pathological gaming), having reached 360 schools and over 1.6 million people.

The European Commission has launched an EU-wide awareness campaign, “End Human Trafficking. Break the Invisible Chain,” to make human trafficking more visible and help people recognize and report it. The Commission notes that around 10,000 victims are identified each year in the EU, while many more may go undetected; victims can be EU citizens or non-EU nationals and may be exploited for sex, labour, forced criminality, or other forms of trafficking. The campaign encourages the public to learn key warning signs, know where to report suspected cases, and share multilingual materials to help victims access support.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott directed state cybersecurity and health agencies — and state-owned medical facilities — to mitigate cyber risks tied to Chinese-manufactured patient monitoring devices, citing recent CISA and FDA warnings about vulnerabilities that could allow unauthorized access to sensitive medical/personal data; his orders include reviewing all state facilities, cataloging data-transmitting devices, tightening policies protecting health information, and ensuring future purchases comply with a prior state restriction on tech from “adversarial” nations, while specifically flagging Contec CMS8000 and Epsimed MN-120 as prohibited; agencies must comply by April 17, and Abbott signaled he will seek new legislation next session to further protect Texans’ medical data.

The Subang Jaya City Council has launched SENSA (Smart Sensor Awareness), an AI-and-sensor pedestrian safety pilot installed at a high-traffic school-zone crossing to reduce accident risk by detecting pedestrians in real time and automatically triggering multi-sensory warnings—AI-enabled cameras identify crossing behavior, then activate audible horn speakers plus blue LED visual alerts to warn both drivers and pedestrians; the setup also provides 24/7 camera monitoring to support broader safety and traffic-behavior analysis, runs on solar power to improve energy efficiency, and is designed to be portable/modular so it can be rolled out to other high-risk crossings, with the council planning phased expansion based on pilot performance data.

The UK National Audit Office says HMRC’s Large Business directorate is delivering strong value: it manages about 2,000 large/complex business groups that contribute roughly two-fifths of HMRC’s receipts, using a “co-operative compliance” model built around dedicated Customer Compliance Managers (CCMs). The NAO reports the large-business tax gap has trended down from £7.5bn (1.7%) in 2005-06 to £5.8bn (0.7%) in 2023-24, while compliance yield nearly doubled to £15.8bn between 2021-22 and 2024-25—about £95 returned per £1 spent on staff pay (vs £25 across HMRC compliance overall). Large businesses also report higher satisfaction, with 91% rating their relationship with their CCM as good (2024). HMRC is exploring extending this approach to more (mid-sized) businesses, and the NAO recommends detailed planning and cost-benefit analysis, including the impact on businesses’ resources.

HMRC has launched the Tax Confident campaign to help people understand the basics of tax – “what tax is, how it works, and why it matters”. An accompanying toolkit includes website and newsletter copy and social media posts for use by stakeholders interested in supporting the campaign.

R&D and creative interdisciplinary projects
HMRC has updated its guidance on the definition of R&D for tax purposes to cover creative interdisciplinary projects. HMRC says that the updated guidance “clarifies that the costs associated with arts related roles and activities may qualify [for R&D tax relief] where they directly contribute to resolving scientific or technological uncertainties”.

new Judicial AI Consortium, launched by judges in Colorado, Texas and Louisiana, is bringing state and federal judges together to share practical experiences and concerns as generative AI enters U.S. courtrooms; with about 90 judges already interested, the group’s goal is not to impose one-size-fits-all rules but to exchange resources on issues like appropriate in-chambers use, risks such as AI “hallucinations” and deepfake evidence, especially after incidents where staff use of AI in drafting orders led to errors and congressional scrutiny, highlighting a perceived “information vacuum” about what tools exist and how to use them responsibly.

Karnataka has launched a pilot e-courts initiative to make court proceedings paperless and more citizen-centric, starting in Mysuru, Bengaluru, Kalaburagi and Dharwad, with infrastructure being set up in both new and existing court complexes, staff recruitment planned, and training to be provided for e-filing; the state has allocated ₹10 crore for the pilot, which aims to digitise case records, filings and daily proceedings to cut delays, improve transparency and accountability, speed up access to case information for litigants and lawyers, and strengthen record storage and retrieval before scaling statewide

Vietnam’s National Assembly passed Law No. 150/2025/QH15 on Specialized Courts for International Financial Centers (IFCs) on 11 Dec 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026, creating a ring-fenced dispute resolution system for IFCs in Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang: a dedicated court in HCMC (first instance + appellate) with exclusive jurisdiction over certain investment/business disputes and arbitration/judgment recognition matters involving an IFC member (excluding public/state interest cases), with final appellate judgments (no cassation/retrial), foreign judges allowed (mixed panels; 10+ years’ expertise; English proficiency), English as a functional language, flexible “Specialized Rules of Procedure” (notably no procuracy participation), broader party autonomy to choose foreign law/customs for foreign-element contracts (subject to Vietnam’s “public order,” and not for real-estate rights where lex situs applies), an extendable/agreeable limitation period up to 6 years, plus strong implementation tools: a full e-court system, direct enforcement by an enforcement judge (asset freeze/seizure/exit restrictions), and judicial immunity (except intentional serious violations); practical impact will depend on forthcoming guidance—especially how “public order” is defined—so businesses dealing with IFC members should review dispute resolution clauses to leverage the new mechanism.

New York lawmakers are considering Senate Bill S7263, which would ban AI chatbots from giving legal or medical advice in ways that could amount to impersonating licensed professionals or enabling the unauthorized practice of law/medicine. The bill would require a clear, conspicuous disclosure that the user is interacting with an AI system (in the same language and readable font), and it would create a private right of action, letting users sue chatbot owners for damages and attorneys’ fees if the ban is violated—meaning enforcement wouldn’t rely only on government action. The proposal is part of a broader package that also includes measures on child safety in chatbots, notices for generative AI, and rules around biometric data and synthetic content, and it would take effect 90 days after the governor signs it.

New York’s RAISE Act (Responsible AI Safety and Education Act), signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul on Dec. 22, 2025, introduces stricter AI governance by requiring large “frontier” AI developers to publish their safety protocols and report any safety incidents to the state within 72 hours of discovery; it also creates a dedicated oversight office inside the New York Department of Financial Services to evaluate major developers and issue annual public reports, while empowering the Attorney General to pursue civil enforcement for noncompliance or false statements, with penalties up to $1 million for a first violation and up to $3 million for subsequent violations—positioning New York alongside states like California that are advancing transparency-focused AI regulation even as federal actions and debates create uncertainty about how far states can go.
